name: Unionism in Ireland
summary: Irish unionism holds that Ireland, and since 1921 Northern Ireland, should remain part of the United Kingdom under the Crown, and opposes Home Rule and Irish unification. It rests on loyalty to the Crown and Constitution, equal citizenship, British identity and the consent of Northern Ireland's majority. Its strands differ on power-sharing, the Irish language and how British or Ulster-centred the community is.
scope: Its position on the national question only: union with Great Britain, the Crown, British and Ulster identity, consent, the border and Dublin's role, language and culture, minorities and the means it accepts. Drawn from the 1892 Convention, the 1912 Covenant, the Ulster Unionist Council's decisions to 1920, and the UUP, DUP and TUV statements from 1969 to 2022. Party programmes on the economy, welfare, social and moral policy are borrowing and are not counted. It excludes paramilitary loyalism and Southern and Catholic unionism.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Covenant pledges its signers as loyal subjects of the King, and the 1892 Ulster Convention declared devoted loyalty to the Crown and Constitution of the United Kingdom.

elective-rulers.rationale: Unionism is loyal to the hereditary Crown in the Covenant and the 1892 resolution, and scholarship names the monarchy as a core object of civic unionism, so choosing the head of state by election instead of inheritance contradicts it.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Unionism pledges loyalty to the Crown as head of state (Covenant, 1892 Convention), which an elected head of state would replace.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The DUP and TUV make defending British identity, culture and way of life central (refusing to be made ashamed of it, a cultural security agenda, support for the Loyal Orders' and marching traditions), and scholarship records unionism as defending a British cultural commonality.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Unionist programmes proclaim the right of all citizens to equal treatment under the law, and the DUP's founding principle is that all are equal under the law and equally subject to it; the Covenant claims equal citizenship.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Northern Ireland's status, unionists hold, can change only if a majority of its people vote for it: the UUP calls the consent principle established and the DUP's seventh test requires majority consent for any diminution of its place in the UK.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The DUP says political authority must derive from the people and its test requires that Northern Ireland's people have a say in the laws that govern them; the Covenant refuses to recognise a parliament imposed on Ulster.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The UUP accepted a power-sharing executive in 1998 and the DUP later proposed cross-community key votes and was ready to enter an executive, but the DUP opposed it in 1998 and the TUV holds that devolution with Sinn Fein in government is antithetical to the Union.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The UUP defends the fiscal unity of the Kingdom and the financial arrangements of the Union that underpin Northern Ireland's social security, and the DUP argues the Union gives a standard of living a united Ireland could not.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The DUP leader says unionism is open to all whatever their class, religion or ethnicity, and speaks of welcoming new identities and of the diversity of the UK's peoples, and the UUP presents the Union as an accommodating plural state.

religious-nation.rationale: Unionist texts claim to unite Unionists of every creed and say religion does not matter to the Union, though scholarship records a strand that treats the Union as guarding Protestant religio-cultural hegemony.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The UUP says equality of opportunity must never be sacrificed to a supposed equal outcome and opposes positive discrimination in employment, and the DUP and TUV promise to resist any return to 50:50 recruitment.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The UUP says illegal arsenals have no place in a democracy and demands the dismantling of paramilitary structures, republican and loyalist, though unionism itself raised the Ulster Volunteers in 1913.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Covenant pledged all means necessary against Home Rule and unionism raised an armed force in 1913, while modern unionist programmes demand exclusively peaceful and democratic means of all office holders.

right-to-secede.rationale: Unionism opposed Ireland's separation from the United Kingdom, yet accepts that Northern Ireland may leave it if a majority votes, and in 1912-20 claimed Ulster's right to stay out of a Dublin parliament.

minority-language-support.rationale: The DUP promotes Ulster Scots and says it has nothing to fear from the Irish language while rejecting one-sided demands, the UUP accepted the Agreement's language commitments, and the TUV opposes Irish language legislation.

more-religion-public.rationale: Scholarship records a fundamentalist evangelical strand of unionism alongside a secular rationalist one.

missingStatements.text: Citizens in every part of a state should hold the same rights, privileges and status as citizens elsewhere in it.
missingStatements.rationale: The Covenant defends 'equal citizenship in the United Kingdom', and the DUP's first test is that everyone in the UK is entitled to the same privileges (Article 6 of the Acts of Union).

missingStatements.text: A state should not give a neighbouring government a formal role in governing part of its territory.
missingStatements.rationale: The UUP wanted the Anglo-Irish Agreement replaced and the DUP demands that any relationship with the Republic be fully accountable to the Assembly and a settlement within the UK.

notes: Searched, theme by theme: constitutional status and consent (1892 Convention, Covenant, Agreement, UUP and DUP manifestos), Crown and monarchy, Dublin's role and the Republic's claim, Protocol and sovereignty (DUP and TUV 2022), identity, culture, flags, parades, language (DUP 2001, 2017, 2022, TUV 2022), minorities and employment equity, power-sharing and devolution, violence and paramilitary arms, and scholarship (Cochrane). Economy, welfare, morality, ecology, technology and most world questions are party programme and are left null. Strands differ: the UUP accepted the 1998 Agreement and power-sharing, the DUP opposed it then and later accepted devolution on conditions, the TUV rejects devolution with Sinn Fein. The DUP's and TUV's EU sovereignty complaints concern the Protocol and do not settle the statement on pooling sovereignty. The main gap is a unionist party's own constitution or the Ulster Unionist Council's later programmes, and primary texts on the 2016 Brexit positions.
